title: A Retry-After rewritten around two unchanged refill helpers, proved equal in a second
summary: The wait a refused request is told to make is rewritten from `credited + period - now` to `period - (now - credited)`, around the two refill helpers it calls and leaves alone. Each helper holds a 64-bit division, and relating two copies of each across the versions is more than the solver settles in a minute. The proof takes the unchanged helpers as one function in both versions, never sees their arithmetic, and is done in a second.

change.description: Write the wait as the javadoc says it: `periodNanos - (nowNanos - credited)`, the period less the time since the credit, with the credited time in a local, instead of `lastAfter(...) + periodNanos - nowNanos`. The check that a token is there, and the two calls into `TokenBucket`, stay as they were.

risk: None: the two expressions are the same arithmetic in two's complement, and the pull request says so. What is at stake is the cost of knowing it. A regression proof of this method has to relate what each version computes from `tokensAfter` and `lastAfter`, and each of those divides a 64-bit difference by the period: the solver is handed two copies of each division, one per version, and asked whether the sums around them agree, which it had not settled after a minute. A proof that times out is a proof nobody runs on the next pull request.
explanation: Before any solver runs, the tool compares the two versions' bytecode. The target changed, so there is something to prove; but `TokenBucket.tokensAfter` and `TokenBucket.lastAfter` are called by both versions, are identical in both, and are pure functions of their five `long` arguments: no field, no array, nothing of the JDK beyond `Math.min`. Each is taken as one function in both versions, as relational verification does with an uninterpreted function: a generated stub keeps, per helper, the outcomes it gave, returns them again on the same arguments, and gives new arguments an arbitrary result or the `ArithmeticException` the division can throw; the calls of both versions are redirected to it. What the solver then proves is that with `t` for `tokensAfter(...)` and `c` for `lastAfter(...)`, `t > 0 ? 0 : c + p - now` equals `t > 0 ? 0 : p - (now - c)` for every `t`, `c`, `p` and `now`, which is the ring arithmetic of 64-bit integers and takes it a second. The divisions are never bit-blasted. The proof is sound because the stub can behave as every function the helpers could be, the helpers themselves included; had the rewrite depended on what the helpers actually compute, the solver would have found a counterexample on the stub, the tool would have replayed it through the real bytecode, seen it not reproduce, and run the proof again with the helpers as written.
resolution: Merge. The proof line names the helpers it took as one function, which is what a reviewer checks: that the change is indeed around them and not in them.
notes: On the machine the examples are measured on (JBMC 6.11.0, CaDiCaL), the proof with the helpers shared took 1.3 s over all 2^320 inputs. With `--no-shared-callees`, the search over inputs in [0:20] passed in a second and the search over [-100000:100000] had not finished after 60 s: two 64-bit divisions and two remainders, one of each per version, compared across the versions.

The helpers are shared because both versions call them, their bytecode is identical in both (constant pool references resolved, so a renumbered pool does not count), and they are pure functions of primitives. A helper that reads a field, takes an array, or calls into the JDK beyond its arithmetic is proved as written, as before.

The stub throws what the helper can throw, here `ArithmeticException` from the division, chosen arbitrarily per new arguments: a version that catches it where the other does not is still found to differ (the library's tests cover that case).

A counterexample found on the stub is replayed through the real bytecode first. One that does not reproduce means the rewrite depends on the helpers' arithmetic; the tool says so in a `note:` line and proves the method again with the helpers as written, which for a 64-bit division may still be the time-out this example avoids.

Since this example was written, the tool's own checker (`--engine native`, examples 124 and 125) proves the change with the helpers as written, in 1.1 s over three paths and three solver calls (0.3 s since the checker leaves a division to the solver under cheap facts and builds its circuit only where a model got it wrong: here never, `0 of 1 divisions and 0 of 0 multiplications built in full` in its log): in it both versions' calls of a helper on the same arguments are the same gates, by the hashing that makes one circuit of one function of the same bits, so the solver never compares two division circuits, which is what the shared-callee stubs achieve for JBMC. That is the library's run of this shape (`--engine native --no-shared-callees`), not the pipeline's; examples 132 and 133 are regression proofs of the refill helper itself by the checker.
provenance: Constructed on the Retry-After kernel of Crosscut's rate limiter, which calls the two refill helpers of example 031; the rewrite is the one that makes the code read as its own javadoc. The technique is the uninterpreted-function abstraction of unchanged callees that regression verification rests on.

references.title: Godlin and Strichman, Regression verification: proving the equivalence of similar programs (2013)
